newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Bildt warns Serbia, calls for full democracy.
newsitem.headline: Bildt warns Serbia, calls for full democracy.

text.p: Serbia must adopt radical democratic reforms and President Slobodan Milosevic should drop a threat to crack down on huge street demonstrations, international peace coordinator Carl Bildt said on Monday.

Bildt's outspoken comments won qualified support from Washington at a European security summit, with a senior U.S. official saying there could not be a "decent peace in the Balkans" unless Serbia became an open and democratic society.

Bildt, who is coordinating civilian peace efforts in Bosnia, said in a statement issued in Lisbon he was "deeply worried" by the political crisis in Belgrade since it could have an effect on efforts to bring stability to all of former Yugoslavia.
Although Western countries have criticised Milosevic, none has yet called on him openly to ditch the authoritarian form of government which has held him in power for nine years.

Milosevic was a key figure in ending the Bosnian war one year ago and major powers feel they still need his support to make sure the peace lasts. The Serbian socialist leader now faces an unprecedented challenge to his rule at home.

"It is in the interest of the long-term stability of all the region that there is a rapid move towards radical political and economic reform in Serbia...paving the way for a democratic society and a free economy," said Bildt.
"If Serbia is to avoid a crisis which will grow worse and worse, this is the way which Serbia and its people must go."
Bildt said the threats to crack down on protests were "genuinely alarming" as a sign that Milosevic could be ready to use force as he did to quell protests in 1991.
"If the authorities were now to try and stop the protests through violence...it would dramatically increase the distance between the regime in Belgrade and the international community," he said.
A senior U.S. official, who asked not to be identified, told reporters Washington acknowledged "the nature of the regime" despite the Serbian leader's important role in helping end the war in Bosnia.

"While President Milosevic and Serbia were an integral part of those negotiations...we believe that there cannot be a decent peace in the Balkans without an open and prosperous and democratic Serbia," the official said.
Britain and France called on Monday for calm and said they were disturbed by talk of a government crackdown. But neither urged Milosevic to adopt radical reforms and ditch his system.

Yugoslavia -- comprising Serbia and Montenegro -- is not at the European security summit of more than 50 nations. Its membership in the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) was suspended in 1992.
At that time, the war in Bosnia was raging and Milosevic was branded a warmonger by the international community.
In Belgrade on Monday, opposition and student leaders denounced the government's threat of a crackdown after two weeks of protests that show no sign of fading away.
Police and city authorities warned on Sunday they would stop tolerating demonstrations in Belgrade which have drawn up to 100,000 protesters a day.
The two-day Lisbon summit will approve a continued role for the OSCE in former Yugoslavia, where it monitors human rights, helps with elections in Bosnia and organises arms control.
